passages.text: Human decisions about when to act originate within a basal forebrain-nigral circuit
Significance

Decision-making studies often focus on brain mechanisms for selecting between goals and actions; however, another important, and often neglected, aspect of decision-making in humans concerns whether, at any given point in time, it is worth making any action at all. <sentence_start/>We showed that a considerable portion of the variance in when voluntary actions are emitted can be explained by a simple model that that takes into account key features of the current environment. <sentence_start/>By using ultrahigh-field MRI we identified a multilayered circuit in the human brain originating far beyond the medial frontal areas typically linked to human voluntary action starting in the basal forebrain and brain stem, converging in the dopaminergic midbrain, and only then projecting to striatum and cortex.

Decisions about when to act are critical for survival in humans as in animals, but how a desire is translated into the decision that an action is worth taking at any particular point in time is incompletely understood. <sentence_start/>Here we show that a simple model developed to explain when animals decide it is worth taking an action also explains a significant portion of the variance in timing observed when humans take voluntary actions. <sentence_start/>The model focuses on the current environment’s potential for reward, the timing of the individual’s own recent actions, and the outcomes of those actions. <sentence_start/>We show, by using ultrahigh-field MRI scanning, that in addition to anterior cingulate cortex within medial frontal cortex, a group of subcortical structures including striatum, substantia nigra, basal forebrain (BF), pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN), and habenula (HB) encode trial-by-trial variation in action time. <sentence_start/>Further analysis of the activity patterns found in each area together with psychophysiological interaction analysis and structural equation modeling suggested a model in which BF integrates contextual information that will influence the decision about when to act and communicates this information, in parallel with PPN and HB influences, to nigrostriatal circuits. <sentence_start/>It is then in the nigrostriatal circuit that action initiation per se begins.

Flexible behavior involves not only choosing the right action but also initiating the chosen action at just the right moment. <sentence_start/>For example, a hunting animal must strike at just the right time, when it is close enough to reach its prey before it has a chance to escape but when it is still far enough away to avoid detection. <sentence_start/>The same is true in humans; an art collector may choose to bid for a specific item in an auction, but it is also important to place the bid at the right moment, when other bidders will not have a chance to outbid, but still leave enough time to place a bid. <sentence_start/>The ability to initiate self-timed actions is vital to animals’ survival, and the consequences of its disruption can be observed in neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s disease. <sentence_start/>It is well established that free voluntary choices in humans depend in some way on a brain region somewhere in the medial frontal cortex, but an explanation of why decisions to act emerge at particular points in time has been lacking (<citation rid="r1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19020512" doi="10.1038/nrn2497" count="1">1<citation rid="r2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28966084" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2017.09.057" pmcid="PMC5737384" count="1"><citation rid="r3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="14976320" doi="10.1126/science.1090973" count="1" /></citation></citation>-<citation rid="r4" ref-type="bibr" count="1">4</citation>).

We have recently shown in macaques that a circuit comprising anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and basal forebrain (BF) integrates past and present contextual information that influences when an action is made (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the interplay between BF and other brain circuits involved in the generation of self-initiated actions remains unclear. <sentence_start/>Basal ganglia, in particular, play a major role in different aspects of action selection and initiation (<citation rid="r6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27012960" doi="10.1016/j.conb.2016.02.005" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="r7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31018098" doi="10.1146/annurev-neuro-072116-031033" count="1">7</citation>); activity in many striatal neurons increases prior to action onset (<citation rid="r8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10893428" doi="10.1152/physrev.2000.80.3.953" count="1">8</citation>, <citation rid="r9" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24464039" doi="10.1038/nn.3632" pmcid="PMC3955116" count="1">9</citation>). <sentence_start/>Additionally, activity in substantia nigra (SN) pars compacta (SNc) dopamine neurons, and their terminals in the striatum, has been linked to self-paced action initiation (<citation rid="r10" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27398617" doi="10.1038/nature18942" pmcid="PMC4970879" count="1">10</citation>, <citation rid="r11" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29420469" doi="10.1038/nature25457" count="1">11</citation>). <sentence_start/>Our previous finding that BF mediates the influence of past and present context on the emergence of a decision about when to act might therefore seem surprising, especially given that BF is the major source of cholinergic projection neurons to cortex. <sentence_start/>However, it has been suggested that acetylcholine may also play an independent and complementary role in initiation of self-timed actions (<citation rid="r12" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30920369" doi="10.7554/eLife.44903" pmcid="PMC6457892" count="1">12</citation>). <sentence_start/>For example, the activity of the cholinergic neurons that project from the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) to the SNc dopamine neurons modulates locomotion (<citation rid="r13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27100197" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2016.03.028" pmcid="PMC4840478" count="1">13</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, we still know comparatively little about the interplay between BF and other subcortical nuclei associated with dopamine and the striatum. <sentence_start/>The first major aim of the current study was to elucidate this relationship and to test whether BF integrates information about when an action should be made while activity in interconnected nuclei is linked to the action initiation per se.

The second major aim was to investigate these processes in the human brain. <sentence_start/>We used a behavioral paradigm to investigate in humans how contextual factors and internal state, shaped by present and past environment, are integrated to determine when to act. <sentence_start/>We used ultrahigh-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) of cortical and subcortical structures to identify brain activity mediating decisions about when to act. <sentence_start/>Finally, we used psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analysis and structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the interaction between these structures at a circuit level.

First, behavioral analyses demonstrated that in humans, contextual information influenced apparently voluntary decisions about when to act. <sentence_start/>As in macaques (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>) a large proportion of variance in decisions about when to act could be explained by a quantitative model that deduced what we refer to as a deterministic component of time to act based on features of the environment relating to both current context and the recent past context. <sentence_start/>Second, ultrahigh-field functional imaging identified a group of subcortical structures whose activity was parametrically related to the factors that change the likelihood of action at a given point in time, rather than action initiation per se. <sentence_start/>Third, model-based fMRI analysis showed that as in macaques, blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) activity in BF could be explained by trial-to-trial variation in deterministic action time, which is the predicted action time given present and past contextual factors. <sentence_start/>In addition, however, the current behavioral paradigm also made it possible to identify other patterns of activity more directly linked to action initiation per se in other nuclei. <sentence_start/>Fourth, examination of the patterns of activity interaction across these nuclei, aided by PPI and SEM, allowed us to identify a multilayered circuit in the human brain originating far beyond the medial frontal areas typically linked to human voluntary action initiation, starting in the BF, habenula (HB), and PPN; converging in the dopaminergic SN; and only then projecting to striatum and cortex.
Results
Participants Used Contextual Factors to Decide When to Act.

We developed a task to investigate in humans how contextual factors and internal state, shaped by present and past environment, are integrated to determine when to act. <sentence_start/>Twenty participants were instructed to track stimuli on the screen (bubbles emerging from a draining water tank, one at a time, every 2 s) and to choose a bubble by making a response at a time of their choice (only one bubble could be picked per trial) (Fig. 1 <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">B</italic>). <sentence_start/>Each bubble potentially contained a monetary reward. <sentence_start/>The magnitude and the probability of reward were represented by the color and the size of the bubble, respectively. <sentence_start/>The color and rate of change (slope) in bubble size changed from trial to trial but remained constant within a trial: gold, silver, and bronze bubbles contained large, medium, and small levels of reward; the bubbles got bigger and bigger (higher reward probability) or smaller and smaller (lower reward probability), as the water level was dropping, with different slopes. <sentence_start/>It took 20 s for the whole tank to drain. <sentence_start/>In addition, different levels of noise were added to the linearly changing bubble size: while in some trials it was very easy for participants to track the rate of change in size of the bubbles (reward probability), it was much harder in other trials. <sentence_start/>Together these factors comprised the present contextual factors (Fig. 1<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>) (<italic toggle="yes">Methods</italic>). <sentence_start/>Importantly, they were varied independently of one another and in a pseudorandomized order (Fig. 1<italic toggle="yes">E</italic>). <sentence_start/>Previous investigations have shown that the timing of the next action that a rat or macaque makes is related to the timing of recent previous actions (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="r14" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28521140" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2017.04.040" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, in addition to the present context, we also investigated whether the outcomes and action times of recent past trials influenced human participants’ action time on the current trial. <sentence_start/>These factors comprised the past contextual factors (Fig. 1<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>).

present and past contextual factors. <sentence_start/>The contextual factors were varied from trial-to-trial, independently of one another, and in a pseudorandomized order.

We investigated whether these features of the present and past context influenced when humans decide to act. <sentence_start/>Time to act (<italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>) was indexed as the time passed in seconds from the moment the water level started dropping until the participant made a response. <sentence_start/>On average, participants made a response after 9.75 ± 1.83 s (<italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>). <sentence_start/>A linear mixed-effect model (<italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>) showed a significant interaction between rate of change in reward probability and reward magnitude [β = 0.05 ± 0.02, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>2</sup></italic> (1) = 6.85, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.009] and noise [β = 0.15 ± 0.03, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>2</sup></italic> (1) = 34.29, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.0001]. <sentence_start/>This suggests that participants waited longer before responding when bubbles were getting bigger (positive reward probability slope), but they did so more when offered a large compared to a small reward and when it was easy to track the rate of change in size of the bubbles (low level of noise) (Fig. 2 <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">A</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>). <sentence_start/>Past contextual factors also influenced participants’ <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on the current trial was longer when <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> had been longer on the past trial [β = 0.06 ± 0.03, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>2</sup></italic> (1) = 4.63, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.03; Fig. 2<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>], and it was longer when participants had received a reward compared to no reward on the past trial. <sentence_start/>However, this last effect did not reach significance [β = 0.09 ± 0.05, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>2</sup></italic> (1) = 3.42, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.06; Fig. 2<italic toggle="yes">E</italic>].

SNR, signal-to-noise ratio) (<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>). <sentence_start/>On the <italic toggle="yes">x</italic> axis the rise is the difference between the reward probability in the last (0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, and 1) and first (0.5) bubble, and the run is the time it takes for the whole water tank to drain (20 s). <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">D</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">E</italic>) Effect of past contextual factors on <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>Participants waited longer before responding when they had already delayed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on the past trial (<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>), and it was longer when they had received a reward compared to no reward on the past trial (<italic toggle="yes">E</italic>). <sentence_start/>Error bars show standard error of the mean across participants. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">D</italic>, the shaded area is SE across observations. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">F</italic>) Proportion of explained variance (PEV) in <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> explained by the Cox regression model. <sentence_start/>PEV is estimated separately from present and past, present, and past contextual factors. <sentence_start/>Each ring represents one participant. <sentence_start/>See also <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> .
Contextual Factors Explained a Large Proportion of Variance in Time to Act.

Having shown that contextual factors influence decision time to act, we next used a Cox proportional hazard model to estimate <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, at each trial, from present and past contextual factors (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="r14" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28521140" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2017.04.040" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>Specifically, we asked how much time (in seconds) would pass before a participant decided to respond, given present and past contextual factors. <sentence_start/>To make comparison across species possible we followed the same procedure as previously used to estimate <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> in macaques (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>): First, we estimated Cox regression coefficients for reward magnitude, rate of change in reward probability, and noise on the current trial. <sentence_start/>In addition, we estimated Cox regression coefficients for actual reward outcome and <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on past trials. <sentence_start/>Next, we used the Cox regression coefficients from present and past trial contextual factors (<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> − 1, where <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> is number of trial) to estimate the expected <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> at each trial. <sentence_start/>We refer to the prediction of the model as deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>present</sub> <sub>+</sub> <sub>past</sub> <sub>context</sub>. <sentence_start/>In contrast to the <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> actually observed (observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>), the deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>present</sub> <sub>+</sub> <sub>past</sub> <sub>context</sub> is the time passed, from beginning of the trial, at which the participant is expected to make a response, given the influence that present and past contextual factors are known to have. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, we separately assessed the contribution of past and present context to deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>We used the Cox regression coefficients relating to either the present trial (<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>) or the past trials (<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> - 1, similar to the original model) to derive two separate <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> estimates. <sentence_start/>These new estimates were termed deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>present</sub> <sub>context</sub> and deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>past</sub> <sub>context</sub>.

We then asked what percentage of the trial-to-trial variability in observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> could be explained by present context, past context, or a combination of both contexts (<italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>). <sentence_start/>On average, present and past contextual factors together explained 24 ± 8% of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> variance. <sentence_start/>Of this, 13 ± 9% and 11 ± 4% were explained by present and past contextual factors, respectively (Fig. 2<italic toggle="yes">F</italic>). <sentence_start/>This is lower than in a related paradigm in monkeys (36 ± 9%) (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>) but still a large proportion of variance.
A Subset of Subcortical Structures Encodes Decision Time to Act.

To identify potential subcortical structures that track the parametric variation in action time we examined activity in anatomical regions of interest (ROIs), which have been linked to action initiation (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="r7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31018098" doi="10.1146/annurev-neuro-072116-031033" count="1">7</citation>, <citation rid="r11" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29420469" doi="10.1038/nature25457" count="1">11</citation>, <citation rid="r13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27100197" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2016.03.028" pmcid="PMC4840478" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="r15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20559337" doi="10.1038/nrn2866" pmcid="PMC3447364" count="1">15</citation>, <citation rid="r16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28384477" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2017.02.027" count="1">16</citation>). <sentence_start/>The a priori selected ROIs included caudate nucleus (CN), putamen, nucleus accumbens (NAc), globus pallidus (GP), SN, ventral tegmental area (VTA), PPN, HB, and BF (note that because of the close adjacency of several small and diverse nuclei near the nucleus basalis, our BF region focuses on septal nuclei and part of the diagonal band of Broca) (Fig. 3<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>). <sentence_start/>To investigate whether subcortical structures track the parametric variation in either the empirically observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> recorded on each trial or the deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> at which actions were expected to be made on each trial given the known influence of the environmental context, we created anatomical masks for each ROI and each individual participant (<italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ) and extracted the time course of the neural activation from each ROI, with respect to response onset (<italic toggle="yes">Methods</italic>).

by contrast, SN, PPN, and HB encode <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> long before the initiation of action (average <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> across all conditions and participants is 9.61 s) during an early decision phase when the factors determining action first become observable. <sentence_start/>In support of this, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant interaction effect of decision phase and ROI on group peaks [<italic toggle="yes">F</italic>(5,90) = 2.61, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.03, <italic toggle="yes">η</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sub>p</sub></italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>2</sup></italic> = 0.13] (<italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>), suggesting that parametric variation in observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> was associated with a late, negative BOLD response in CN, NAc, and BF but an early, positive BOLD response in SN, PPN, and HB.

Next, to identify cortical structures outside our anatomical ROIs that could also be involved in encoding of observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> we ran a whole-brain analysis. <sentence_start/>We used a GLM (<italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>, GLM1) to look for brain areas in which activity reflected parametric variation in the empirically observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, separately on trials where rate of change in reward probability was positive (i.e., waiting longer before responding was associated with an increased chance of getting reward; long <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> contrast) and negative (i.e., responding quickly was associated with an increased chance of getting reward; short <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> contrast). <sentence_start/>For the long <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> contrast, the largest cluster was located in the ACC extending into supplementary motor area (SMA) (peak Z = 4.35, Montreal Neurological Institute [MNI] coordinate: <italic toggle="yes">x</italic> = 0, <italic toggle="yes">y</italic> = −4, <italic toggle="yes">z</italic> = 58; whole-brain cluster-based correction, Z > 3.1, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.0001; Fig. 4<italic toggle="yes">A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ). <sentence_start/>For the short <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> contrast, the cluster was located at the striatum (peak Z = 4.42, MNI: <italic toggle="yes">x</italic> = 14, <italic toggle="yes">y</italic> = 8, <italic toggle="yes">z</italic> = −8; whole-brain cluster-based correction, Z > 3.1, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.0001; Fig. 4<italic toggle="yes">B</italic> and <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ). <sentence_start/>Whole-brain analysis suggests that in addition to striatum, which was already part of our a priori selected ROIs, ACC and SMA are also involved in encoding of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>To illustrate the timing of encoding of observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> in ACC and striatum, we extracted the time course of the neural activation in a 14-mm<sup>3</sup> sphere ROI centered on the activation peak with respect to response onset (Fig. 4 <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">C</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">D</italic>). <sentence_start/>In accordance with our previous finding, the effect of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on BOLD signal in striatum peaked during the late decision phase. <sentence_start/>However, this effect peaked during the early decision phase in ACC.

BOLD signal in ACC and striatum is correlated with time to act. <sentence_start/>Whole-brain analysis showing voxels where activity reflected parametric variation in the empirically observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, on trials where rate of change in reward probability was (<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>) positive (<italic toggle="yes">long actTime</italic> was the correct strategy) and (<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>) negative (<italic toggle="yes">short actTime</italic> was the correct strategy). <sentence_start/>Whole-brain cluster-based correction, Z > 3.1. <sentence_start/>(See <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> for the list of clusters.<sentence_start/>) (<italic toggle="yes">C</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">D</italic>) ROI time course analysis of the ACC/SMA (<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>) and striatum (<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>), showing the relationship between BOLD and <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>Time 0 is the response time. <sentence_start/>Note that the hemodynamic lag means that a BOLD signal change reflects neural activity ∼6 s earlier. <sentence_start/>The lines and shadings show the mean and SE of the β weights across the participants, respectively. <sentence_start/>See also <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> .
BF Communicates Decisions About When to Act to Nigrostriatal Pathway.

Time course analyses showed that BOLD response in a subset of our subcortical ROIs is correlated with parametric variation in empirically observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>We next, however, asked 1) whether the same areas integrated contextual factors to compute the deterministic component of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, as estimated by the Cox regression model [specifically, based on our previous finding in macaques (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>), we expected BF to be involved in encoding the deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>-the time at which the response is expected to be made given the known influence of the contextual factors], and 2) whether the same areas encoded action initiation per se, above and beyond the parametric variation in <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>.

To answer the first question, we added deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> to the time series GLM as the variable of interest and the observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> as covariate (<italic toggle="yes">Methods</italic>, GLM2.3). <sentence_start/>We found that deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> explained BOLD activity in BF [<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 3.55, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.02, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 0.81; corrected for multiple comparisons]. <sentence_start/>This was not the case for other ROIs (Fig. 5<italic toggle="yes">A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ). <sentence_start/>This suggests that, as in macaques (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>), BF activity in humans is involved in integrating present and past contextual information to construct the deterministic component of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the effect of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on BF BOLD signal peaked during the early decision phase and was much earlier compared to the effect of observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on BF BOLD (compare Figs. <sentence_start/>3 and 5), and the effect was stronger during early compared to the late decision phase [paired-samples <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test; <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 2.33, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.03, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 0.53] (Fig. 5<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>). <sentence_start/>This suggests, after considering the BOLD hemodynamic lag, that deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> is encoded long before action initiation when the factors determining it become observable. <sentence_start/>Next, we asked whether present and past contextual factors contribute equally to encoding of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> in BF. <sentence_start/>Deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>present</sub> <sub>context</sub> and deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>past</sub> <sub>context</sub> were used in a time series GLM (<italic toggle="yes">Methods</italic>, GLM2.4), with the observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> as covariate. <sentence_start/>BOLD activity in BF was related with deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>present</sub> <sub>context</sub> [<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 4.87, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.001, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 1.12; corrected for multiple comparisons; <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ]. <sentence_start/>This was not true for <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>past</sub> <sub>context</sub> [<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 2.22, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.32; corrected for multiple comparisons<italic toggle="yes">;</italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ]. <sentence_start/>This suggests that BF mostly employed present contextual factors to construct the deterministic component of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> [paired-samples <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test; <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 2.00, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.06, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 0.46] (Fig. 5 <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">C</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">D</italic>).
Fig. 5<sentence_start/>.

BF encodes the deterministic component of time to act. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>) Peak effect of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on ROI BOLD signal. <sentence_start/>Significance testing on time course data was performed by using a leave-one-out procedure on the group peak signal identified within the whole epoch. <sentence_start/>The effect of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on BF BOLD signal seems similar in size to effects in other areas. <sentence_start/>However, compared to other areas, deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> explained BOLD activity in BF in a uniform and consistent manner across participants and therefore in a significant way. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>) Peak effect of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on ROI BOLD signal identified separately within the early decision and late decision phases. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>) Time course analysis of the BF, showing the relationship between BOLD activity and deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> estimated separately from present (deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>present</sub>) and past (deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><sub>past</sub>) context. <sentence_start/>Format is the same as in Fig. 3<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>. (<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>) Peak effect of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sub>present</sub></italic> on ROI BOLD signal, identified within the whole epoch. <sentence_start/>Each ring represents one participant. <sentence_start/>The gray columns illustrate the group mean. <sentence_start/>Paired-samples <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test and one-sample <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction. <sentence_start/>*<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.05, **<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.01. <sentence_start/>See also <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> .

To answer the second question-whether the same areas encoded action initiation per se, above and beyond the parametric variation in <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>-we regressed an unmodulated regressor indexing action initiation against the ROIs’ extracted time series (<italic toggle="yes">Methods</italic>, constant regressor in GLM2.3) and added the deterministic and the observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> as covariates. <sentence_start/>Dopaminergic midbrain [one-sample <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test corrected for multiple comparisons; SN, <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 3.38, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.02, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 0.78; VTA, <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 5.44, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.0003, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 1.25], PPN [<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 5.47, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.0003, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 1.25], and HB [<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 7.56, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.0001, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 1.73] showed a positive peak ∼2 s after initiation of action (Fig. 6 <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">B</italic>), therefore, once the hemodynamic lag is taken into consideration, indicating activity prior to movement onset. <sentence_start/>This effect on BOLD response is constant and does not vary from trial to trial; it thus demonstrates the encoding of action initiation per se rather than parametric variation in observed or deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the BOLD response peaked at the same time in all four areas and showed a gradual ramp-up starting about 3 s before initiation of action, suggesting activity was present during the early decision phase. <sentence_start/>We also observed an effect in CN, putamen, and BF, but the peak occurred much later at about 6 s after the response onset, suggesting activity was present during the late decision phase.
Fig. 6<sentence_start/>.

Dopaminergic midbrain, PPN, and HB encode action initiation per se. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>) ROI time course analysis of the ROIs, showing the relationship between BOLD activity and unmodulated action initiation. <sentence_start/>Format is the same as in Fig. 3<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>. <sentence_start/>The lines and shadings show the mean and SE of the β weights across the participants, respectively. <sentence_start/>Time 0 is the response time. <sentence_start/>Note that the hemodynamic lag means that a BOLD signal change reflects neural activity ∼6 s earlier. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>) Significance testing on time course data was performed by using a leave-one-out procedure on the group peak signal. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>) PPI analysis between BOLD signal in BF and other ROIs, with deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> as the psychological factor. <sentence_start/>Trial by trial variation in the activity in BF was significantly related with trial by trial variation in the activity in SN as a function of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>Significance testing on PPI data was performed by using a leave-one-out procedure on the group peak signal. <sentence_start/>Each ring represents one participant. <sentence_start/>The gray columns illustrate the group mean. <sentence_start/>One-sample <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction. <sentence_start/>*<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.05, ***<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.001.

So far, we have shown that BOLD response in CN, NAc, SN, BF, PPN, and HB is correlated with observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime.</italic> <sentence_start/>Among these areas, however, BF encoded the deterministic component of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> while SN, PPN, and HB encoded the action initiation per se, during the early decision phase. <sentence_start/>We then asked whether BF is functionally connected with SN, PPN, or HB as a function of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime.</italic> <sentence_start/>We performed a PPI analysis (<citation rid="r17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22569188" doi="10.1093/scan/nss055" pmcid="PMC3375893" count="1">17</citation>) (<italic toggle="yes">Methods</italic>, GLM2.5) and found that the functional connectivity between BF and SN is moderated by deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> [one-sample <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test corrected for multiple comparisons; <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 5.76, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.0001, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 1.32]. <sentence_start/>This was not true for the functional connectivity between SN and the other ROIs (Fig. 6<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>). <sentence_start/>Stronger activity in BF was associated with stronger activity in SN as a function of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, compared to functional connectivity between BF and PPN [paired-samples <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test; <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 2.55, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.02, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 0.58] or between BF and HB [<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> (18) = 2.32, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.03, <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 0.53]. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with the BF communicating decisions about when to act to the nigrostriatal pathway. <sentence_start/>It is then within the nigrostriatal circuit or one of the interconnecting areas such as PPN or HB that action initiation per se begins.
Decisions About When to Act Are Constructed Within a Cortico-Subcortical Circuit.

There was a discernible pattern in the type and timing of BOLD signals in subcortical ROIs; the peak effects of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> in BF and observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> in the SN, PPN, and HB tended to arise in the first few seconds of the trial (early decision phase) and were followed by peak effects in striatum just before action initiation (late decision phase). <sentence_start/>Although inferences about the timing of neuronal activity from BOLD response should be treated with caution, the pattern of activity in our ROIs, and previous work on the direct or indirect pathways between them (<citation rid="r7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31018098" doi="10.1146/annurev-neuro-072116-031033" count="1">7</citation>, <citation rid="r15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20559337" doi="10.1038/nrn2866" pmcid="PMC3447364" count="1">15</citation>), is suggestive of a cortico-BF-midbrain-striatal circuit for decisions about when to act. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we tested whether interrelationships in the time series of BOLD signals from our ROIs indicated a circuit within this structure. <sentence_start/>This was done by fitting an SEM to time series data from ROIs that were involved in encoding of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>SEMs define the strength of connections between brain areas in question rather than the degree of activity relating to individual behavioral variables (<italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>). <sentence_start/>As a result, whether or not an individual ROI encodes <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> is orthogonal to the question of its functional interactions with other ROIs.

First, based on the type and timing of BOLD signals in subcortical ROIs, we assumed a model in which activity in CN and NAc is influenced by SN; anatomical connections projecting from SN to CN and NAc and the influence SN exerts on CN and NAc are well known (<citation rid="r18" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25981958" doi="10.1093/brain/awv134" pmcid="PMC4492412" count="1">18</citation>). <sentence_start/>We assumed that activity in SN is influenced by BF in line with the results of our PPI analysis (Fig. 6<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>). <sentence_start/>We also included influences form PPN and HB to SN in line with previously reported monosynaptic projections from PPN and HB to SN (<citation rid="r15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20559337" doi="10.1038/nrn2866" pmcid="PMC3447364" count="1">15</citation>). <sentence_start/>We also included in the model an influence from ACC to BF; BF receives a monosynaptic input from ACC, and they are known to act in concert to determine <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> in monkeys (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="r19" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11274781" doi="10.1016/s0306-4522(00)00585-6" count="1">19</citation>, <citation rid="r20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28747623" doi="10.1038/s41467-017-00072-y" pmcid="PMC5529456" count="1">20</citation>) (Fig. 7<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>; see also <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ). <sentence_start/>Next, we estimated the path coefficients to find out whether the data we had observed would fit the model. <sentence_start/>As predicted, all specified path coefficients in the hypothesized model were significantly different from zero (<italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ) and provided a good description of the data according to at least two of the standard fit indices for structural equation models (standardized root mean square residual = 0.066; goodness-of-fit index = 0.961; root mean square error of approximation = 0.087; <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>).
Fig. 7<sentence_start/>.

Decisions about when to act are constructed within a cortico-subcortical circuit. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>) The hypothesized model in which activity in CN and NAc is influenced by SN; activity in SN is influenced by BF, PPN, and HB; and ACC influences BF (for estimates of path coefficients, see <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ). <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>) Alternative model. <sentence_start/>The hypothesis-driven model fits the data better than an alternative model in which the directions of paths were reversed. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>) Randomly permuting the position of each ROI in the hypothesis-driven model produced a distribution of AICs. <sentence_start/>The AIC of the hypothesis-driven circuit (dashed red line) was positioned in the 0.6th percentile of this distribution. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>) A schematic of a cortico-subcortical circuit for decisions about when to act. <sentence_start/>See also <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> .

Having established that our proposed model fits the observed data well, we compared our model with alternative models and performed a series of control analyses to investigate which connections are influencing the network most. <sentence_start/>First, given that all brain areas have manifold connections, null models presuming no connections between ROIs are unsuitable points of comparison for connectivity analysis (<citation rid="r21" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19226186" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.1000033" pmcid="PMC2642881" count="1">21</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, we compared the hypothesis-driven model to an alternative model in which the direction of connections was reversed (Fig. 7<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>). <sentence_start/>Note that the alternative model therefore has an identical number of degrees of freedom. <sentence_start/>The hypothesis-driven model (Akaike information criterion [AIC] = 377,600.5) provided a better description of the data than the alternative model (AIC = 486,306.6).

Second, to rule out the possibility that the significant path coefficients in the hypothesis-driven model are due to factors unrelated to <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, we compared the hypothesized model against an alternative in which parametric variation in BOLD signal due to observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> was regressed out. <sentence_start/>This was done by convolving the main effect of responding and the parametric <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> (time-locked to response) with the canonical HRF and feeding these variables as inputs to all ROIs-the idea being that any remaining variance after these inputs reflects variance over and above the effects of observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>The hypothesis-driven model (AIC = 377,600.5) provided a better description of the data than the alternative in which <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>-relevant variance was removed (AIC = 673,504.8). <sentence_start/>This supports the idea that the paths shown in the hypothesized model are, indeed, interactions that occur as a function of action timing.

Third, we performed a complementary test by comparing the hypothesis-driven model to other models of equivalent complexity by randomly permuting the position of each ROI in the circuit and obtaining the AIC of each variation. <sentence_start/>Again, this ensures that the alternative models have identical numbers of degrees of freedom. <sentence_start/>This yielded a total of 5,040 models with a median AIC of 389,479.2 (interquartile range = 9,209.4; range = [377,269.6 to 396,045.7]). <sentence_start/>The AIC of the hypothesis-driven model was 377,600.5, which positioned it in the 0.6th percentile of the distribution (Fig. 7<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>).
Discussion

Previous work in humans has identified medial frontal brain areas associated with self-generated, self-timed, or voluntary actions (<citation rid="r1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19020512" doi="10.1038/nrn2497" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="r4" ref-type="bibr" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>Animal studies on the other hand have emphasized the role of basal ganglia circuits (<citation rid="r6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27012960" doi="10.1016/j.conb.2016.02.005" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="r7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31018098" doi="10.1146/annurev-neuro-072116-031033" count="1">7</citation>). <sentence_start/>On the basis of the current results, we propose a circuit comprising structures in medial frontal cortex, basal ganglia, brainstem, and BF, working in concert to encode decisions about when to act and then actually initiating the action (Fig. 7<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>).

Participants performed a behavioral task, while inside an ultrahigh-field MRI scanner. <sentence_start/>They integrated contextual factors, shaped by the present and past environment, that influenced when they would act. <sentence_start/>We then used functional imaging to look for brain activity parametrically related to the factors that determine when might be the right time to make the action. <sentence_start/>We found that activity in ACC, CN, NAc, SN, PPN, HB, and BF encodes parametric variation in <italic toggle="yes">actTime.</italic> <sentence_start/>Self-initiated actions have previously been associated with medial frontal areas such as ACC and SMA (<citation rid="r22" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27090954" doi="10.1146/annurev-neuro-070815-013952" pmcid="PMC5512175" count="1">22<citation rid="r23" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30132759" doi="10.7554/eLife.31826" pmcid="PMC6112854" count="1" /></citation>-<citation rid="r24" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7737391" doi="10.1007/BF00230649" count="1">24</citation>) and basal ganglia such as CN, NAc, and SN (<citation rid="r7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31018098" doi="10.1146/annurev-neuro-072116-031033" count="1">7</citation>, <citation rid="r11" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29420469" doi="10.1038/nature25457" count="1">11</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the possibility that PPN, HB, and BF have roles in self-initiated action has received less attention.

passages.text: BOLD activity in BF was correlated with deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on each trial, providing the first piece of evidence that it was important for action timing. <sentence_start/>The activity change peaked ∼1 s before the actual response was made (Fig. 5<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>). <sentence_start/>Once the hemodynamic lag is taken into account, it is clear that BF activity occurs long before actual initiation of action and instead occurs at the point in time when visual cues indicating the contextual features that would influence action time were first presented. <sentence_start/>This early timing and the fact that-unlike any of the other brain areas investigated-its activity could be explained by the predicted <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> given the influence of present and past contextual factors (deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>) suggest an important role for the BF in mediating the influence of past and present context on decisions about when to act. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with previous studies in macaques (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>).

The SN appears to be an important next stage in the circuit. <sentence_start/>Unlike BF, we did not find any evidence that SN activity reflects the contextual factors influencing when an action was likely to be made; its activity was not significantly related to deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>However, its activity encoded action initiation per se and occurred early in trials prior to movement onset. <sentence_start/>Importantly, PPI analysis showed that functional connectivity between BF and SN was driven by deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>. <sentence_start/>It had been suggested that BF represents combinations of task-relevant contextual variables (<citation rid="r25" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27466331" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1123-16.2016" pmcid="PMC6601885" count="1">25<citation rid="r26" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25972172" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0051-15.2015" pmcid="PMC4429151" count="1"><citation rid="r27" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23666181" doi="10.1038/nn.3398" pmcid="PMC4160807" count="1" /></citation></citation>-<citation rid="r28" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30581022" doi="10.1016/j.cub.2018.11.012" pmcid="PMC6901356" count="1">28</citation>) and encodes decision time to act (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>). However, it was not clear how these representations come to influence action time. Here we observed increased connectivity between BF and SN as a function of deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, consistent with the idea that BF influences the nigrostriatal pathway implicated in self-initiated actions.

toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, and similar to SN, they also encoded action initiation early in the trial. <sentence_start/>However, again unlike BF, we did not find any relation between HB and PPN activity and deterministic <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> suggesting they may exert distinct influences on SN. <sentence_start/>Hikosaka and colleagues describe similar patterns of activity in single neurons of the macaque HB and PPN, both of which encode motivational salience signals in response to newly encountered situations (<citation rid="r29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20624598" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2010.06.016" pmcid="PMC2905384" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="r30" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25058502" doi="10.1016/j.neuroscience.2014.07.002" pmcid="PMC4302061" count="1">30</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the case of HB, these signals covary with the speed of accompanying saccades (<citation rid="r29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20624598" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2010.06.016" pmcid="PMC2905384" count="1">29</citation>), suggesting that early onset activity-like the a<italic toggle="yes">ctTime</italic> signals observed here-might reflect updates to the participants’ estimates of key environmental features at the beginning of each trial (<citation rid="r16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28384477" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2017.02.027" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="r31" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26582981" doi="10.3389/fnbeh.2015.00295" pmcid="PMC4631824" count="1">31</citation>, <citation rid="r32" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28688871" doi="10.1016/j.tins.2017.06.001" pmcid="PMC11568516" count="1">32</citation>). <sentence_start/>These updates might then be translated into adaptive control of downstream SN neurons at or around the time of action initiation. <sentence_start/>The PPN appears important for orienting behavior to the most rewarding course of action because lesions reduce the frequency of win-stay but not lose-shift patterns in rodent behavior (<citation rid="r16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28384477" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2017.02.027" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="r33" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26976089" doi="10.1016/j.nlm.2016.03.010" pmcid="PMC4862904" count="1">33</citation>) (note the relationship between past reward outcome and PPN activity in <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>). <sentence_start/>The HB, in contrast, may be linked to avoidance of negative outcomes and control of impulsive behaviors (<citation rid="r15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20559337" doi="10.1038/nrn2866" pmcid="PMC3447364" count="1">15</citation>) or when a loss or an aversive event is predicted (note the relationship between expected reward on the current trial, <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic>, and HB activity in <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> <italic toggle="yes"> </italic>). <sentence_start/>Lesions of PPN or HB both induce changes in motor behavior, albeit different in nature, that are consistent with roles in action initiation (<citation rid="r34" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23864685" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1568-13.2013" pmcid="PMC6794061" count="1">34<citation rid="r35" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9159502" doi="10.1016/s0304-3940(97)00254-1" count="1"><citation rid="r36" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15562296" doi="10.1038/sj.npp.1300595" count="1" /></citation></citation>-<citation rid="r37" ref-type="bibr" pmid="3178997" doi="10.1016/0166-4328(88)90169-6" count="1">37</citation>).

Dopaminergic pathways have usually been associated with self-initiated action (<citation rid="r11" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29420469" doi="10.1038/nature25457" count="1">11</citation>, <citation rid="r38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29760524" doi="10.1038/s41593-018-0152-y" pmcid="PMC6358212" count="1">38</citation>). <sentence_start/>It is therefore noteworthy that two of the ROIs involved in action timing are distinguished by their cholinergic nature: the PPN, as a principal source of acetylcholine to the basal ganglia (<citation rid="r39" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24671996" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.5071-13.2014" pmcid="PMC3965779" count="1">39</citation>), and the BF, which is implicated in cholinergic neuromodulation of the cortex (<citation rid="r40" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28199851" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2017.01.060" pmcid="PMC5725195" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="r41" ref-type="bibr" pmid="6841683" doi="10.1002/cne.902140206" count="1">41</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, there is evidence for acetylcholine’s involvement in self-initiated action: The bradykinetic deficits of Parkinsonism are accompanied by degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the PPN (<citation rid="r42" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10960043" doi="10.1093/brain/123.9.1767" count="1">42</citation>), and the same population is important in PPN’s interactions with the nigrostriatal pathway (<citation rid="r13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27100197" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2016.03.028" pmcid="PMC4840478" count="1">13</citation>).

Even though ultrahigh-field fMRI enabled us to extract BOLD signals from small structures in the BF, midbrain, and brainstem that would not have been possible with conventional methods, there are still limits to its spatial resolution and thus our ability to distinguish different neural populations. <sentence_start/>SN, for example, consists of the pars compacta and pars reticulata subdivisions that contribute to functionally distinct basal ganglia pathways (<citation rid="r18" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25981958" doi="10.1093/brain/awv134" pmcid="PMC4492412" count="1">18</citation>), which we did not discriminate. <sentence_start/>BF includes various structures and nuclei such as the medial septal nucleus, diagonal nucleus, and nucleus basalis. <sentence_start/>However, because of the close adjacency of several small and diverse nuclei near the nucleus basalis, our BF region focuses on medial septal and diagonal nuclei (but see <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ). <sentence_start/>While neurophysiological recording is necessary for making such comparisons, fMRI can provide a simultaneous overview of activity across a distributed circuit.

Given the direct and indirect paths that are known to exist within basal ganglia circuits and the findings from our time course analyses, we proposed a circuit in which striatum is influenced by SN and SN is influenced by BF, PPN, and HB. <sentence_start/>We used structural equation modeling to verify the plausibility of such a circuit. <sentence_start/>We found that our hypothesized model fits the data well and performs better than alternative models (Fig. 7 and <italic toggle="yes"> </italic> ). <sentence_start/>We do not, however, claim to be proposing a comprehensive model containing all functional connections between subcortical structures. <sentence_start/>There are, of course, other anatomically reasonable connections between structures of our proposed circuit, such as direct influences of the ACC onto SN and HB. <sentence_start/>However, we believe that our proposed model is the simplest anatomically plausible model that can explain our data well. <sentence_start/>We suggest that BF integrates past and present contextual information that will influence the decision about when an action should be made and communicates this information to nigrostriatal circuit (Fig. 6). <sentence_start/>It is then in the nigrostriatal circuit or one of the interconnecting areas such as PPN or HB that action initiation per se begins. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, medial frontal areas such as ACC might provide BF with contextual information it needs to guide decision time (Fig. 4) (<citation rid="r5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2019.10.030" pmcid="PMC6975166" pmid="31813653" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="r20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28747623" doi="10.1038/s41467-017-00072-y" pmcid="PMC5529456" count="1">20</citation>). <sentence_start/>We found an influence from ACC to BF that may correspond with such a possibility during circuit-level analysis (Fig. 7).
Methods
Subjects.

Twenty participants (15 females), aged 19 to 34 y, completed the study. <sentence_start/>All participants were paid £10 per h for participating in the study and additional £3 to 7 for performance-dependent reward collected during the task. <sentence_start/>Each participant provided written informed consent at the beginning of the testing session. <sentence_start/>Ethical approval was given by the Oxford University Central University Research Ethics Committee (Ref-Number MSD-IDREC- /RE001). <sentence_start/>One person was excluded from all neural analyses due to excessive head motion (absolute mean displacement > 2 mm). <sentence_start/>Behavioral data from all participants were included in analyses.
ROI Time Course Analyses.

Anatomical ROIs were created in four stages for subcortical structures: 1) Anatomical masks were designed for each ROI in the MNI standard space using the Harvard-Oxford Subcortical Structural Atlas and Atlas of the Human Brain (<citation rid="r43" ref-type="bibr" count="1">43</citation>). <sentence_start/>2) Masks were transformed from the standard space to each participant’s structural space by applying a standard-to-structural warp that was then thresholded, and binarized. <sentence_start/>3) To make sure that the masks still match the ROIs’ boundaries after unwarping, they were manually edited within each participant’s structural space using FSLeyes. <sentence_start/>4) Masks were transformed from the individual structural to functional space by applying a structural-to-functional warp, thresholded, binarized, and dilated by 1 voxel. <sentence_start/>Functional ROI (ACC and striatum) were defined as spheres of 1.5 mm radius, centered at the peak of the activation of a contrast. <sentence_start/>To avoid any circularity in analyses, functional ROIs were not used in time series analysis of <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> contrast.

For time series analyses, the filtered time series of each voxel within each ROI was averaged, normalized, and up-sampled. <sentence_start/>The up-sampled data were then epoched in 15-s windows, starting from 9 s before to 6 s after the response time. <sentence_start/>Time series GLMs were then fit at each time step of the epoched data, using ordinary least squares. <sentence_start/>We ran the following GLMs:

Leave-One-Out Analysis on Time Series Group Peak Signal.

Significance testing on time course data was performed by using a leave-one-out procedure on the group peak signal to avoid potential temporal selection biases. <sentence_start/>For every participant, we estimated the peak signal time by identifying the peak in the time course of the mean beta weights of the relevant regressor in all other participants. <sentence_start/>When we did this, we identified the peak (positive or negative) of the regressor of interest within the full width of the epoched time course: from 9 s before to 6 s after the response. <sentence_start/>Next, we took the beta weight of the remaining participant at the time of the group peak. <sentence_start/>We repeated this for all participants. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the resulting 19 peak beta weights were selected independently from the time course of each single participant. <sentence_start/>We assessed significance using <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> tests on the resulting peak beta weights. <sentence_start/>To control for familywise error rate the significance level was adjusted for the number of ROIs, using the Holm-Bonferroni method (<citation rid="r44" ref-type="bibr" count="1">44</citation>). <sentence_start/>The effect of observed <italic toggle="yes">actTime</italic> on BOLD activity peaked 4.66 s after the response in one group of ROIs and 1.04 s before the response in another group. <sentence_start/>To further assess the significance of this timing difference we identified the (positive or negative) group peak within an early decision phase defined as a 2-s window before response and within a late decision phase defined as a 2-s window staring 4 s after the response. <sentence_start/>A leave-one-out procedure was used to identify group peak signals in both early and late decision phase.
